content: Reduced uterine blood flow caused by maternal hypotension is a potential contributor to fetal heart rate changes, which are commonly observed following regional analgesia, such as epidural, spinal, or combined spinal-epidural (CSE) techniques, during labor. Administering intravenous fluids prophylactically before regional analgesia may mitigate maternal hypotension. Additionally, using lower doses of local anesthetics or opioid-only blocks may reduce the necessity for such preloading. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of prophylactic intravenous fluid preloading on maternal and fetal outcomes during labor when regional analgesia is employed. The search for relevant studies was conducted through the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, with the initial search completed on February 19, 2004, and an updated search performed on June 30, 2010. The updated results were added to the awaiting classification section of the review. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared prophylactic intravenous preloading before regional analgesia with a control group (either a placebo or no preloading). Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated their quality, and extracted data. Six studies involving a total of 473 participants were included in the analysis. In one trial involving epidural analgesia with high-dose local anesthetics, preloading with intravenous fluids was found to significantly reduce the incidence of maternal hypotension (relative risk [RR] 0.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 0.53; 102 women). This trial also demonstrated a reduction in fetal heart rate abnormalities (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.83; 102 women). However, no significant differences were observed in other maternal or perinatal outcomes in this trial or another trial involving high-dose epidural analgesia. In two trials that used low-dose epidural analgesia, no significant reduction in maternal hypotension was observed (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.48; 260 women). These trials were underpowered to detect anything less than a very large effect. Similarly, no significant differences were found between groups in terms of fetal heart rate abnormalities (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.05; 233 women). In the two trials involving CSE analgesia, no differences were reported between the preloading and no preloading groups. In a trial that used spinal analgesia with opioids, the relative risk for maternal hypotension was 0.89 (95% CI 0.43 to 1.83; 40 women), and the relative risk for fetal heart rate abnormalities was 0.70 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.37; 32 women). In a study that used opioid-only analgesia (30 women), no cases of maternal hypotension or fetal heart rate abnormalities were observed in either group. The authors concluded that preloading with intravenous fluids prior to traditional high-dose local anesthetic blocks may provide some benefits for maternal and fetal outcomes in healthy women. However, the use of low-dose epidural or CSE analgesia techniques may reduce the need for preloading. The included studies were too small to determine whether preloading is beneficial for women receiving regional analgesia during labor with lower-dose local anesthetics or opioids. Further research is needed to investigate the risks and benefits of intravenous preloading in women undergoing low-dose epidural or CSE analgesia, including opioid-only techniques, particularly in those with pregnancy complications. It is noted that five citations in the awaiting classification section of the review may influence the conclusions once they are assessed.
